summary: This document defines a DHCPv6 Client Link-Layer Address option. It specifies the format and mechanism for encoding a client's link-layer address in DHCPv6 Relay-Forward messages.

eli5.summary: When a helper forwards a request, this lets it add the sender's hardware address, like writing a return address on a forwarded letter.

questions: how relay passes client mac address in dhcpv6
how does a dhcpv6 relay pass the client mac address
why correlate dhcpv4 and dhcpv6 clients
subtitle: A DHCPv6 relay option that tells the server the MAC address of the client behind the relay.

tldr.problem: DHCPv4 servers often key their lease database on the client's link-layer address, but DHCPv6 has no simple way to tell a distant server that address, so operators cannot match a client's DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 activity.
tldr.mechanism: A first-hop DHCPv6 relay agent MAY add the Client Link-Layer Address option (code 79) to the Relay-Forward messages it sends, carrying a link-layer type and the client's link-layer address.
tldr.outcome: Servers that choose to use it can correlate dual-stack clients and get extra detail for debugging and logging. Clients never see or send the option.

today: RFC 6939 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The option remains the defined way for a first-hop relay to pass the client link-layer address to a DHCPv6 server.

sections.title: The Dual-Stack Identification Problem
sections.content:
The DHCPv4 header has htype and chaddr fields for the client's link-layer address type and address. In some deployments DHCPv4 servers use chaddr as a customer identifier and as a key into the client lease database.

With IPv6 added to existing IPv4 networks, devices become both DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 clients, and operators need to associate both kinds of message with the same client interface. The link-layer address is an identifier common to that interface.

RFC 3315 does not give a way to tell a DHCP server the client's link-layer address when the server is not on the client's link. Clients send a DHCP Unique Identifier (DUID), but that does not give a simple way to extract the link-layer address. RFC 4361 describes using the same DUID in both protocols, but needs changes to DHCPv4 clients and, per this RFC, has not seen broad adoption.
sections.eli5: The old system sorts customers by hardware address, and the new one does not pass it along. Operators need a way to know the two requests came from the same device.

sections.title: The Client Link-Layer Address Option
sections.content:
The option has an option code, an option length and two data parts. The link-layer type is 16 bits and MUST be a valid hardware type assigned by IANA, as described in RFC 826. The link-layer address is variable length.

  • option-code: OPTION_CLIENT_LINKLAYER_ADDR (79)
  • option-length: 2 plus the length of the link-layer address
sections.eli5: The note says what kind of hardware address it is, then gives the address itself.

sections.title: Relay Agent and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 relay agent that receives a message from a client (for example Solicit or Request, but not Relay-Forward or Advertise) MAY put the message's link-layer source address in the option, in the Relay-Forward messages it sends. Whether it does so can depend on configuration.

A server configured to store or use a client link-layer address SHOULD look for the option in the Relay-Forward message of the relay agent closest to the client. The option is not needed when the server is on the client's own link, since the server can read the address from the link-layer header. If the option appears in anything that is not a Relay-Forward message, the server MUST silently ignore it. A server is not required to return the option in a downstream message.
sections.eli5: The first helper next to you writes your hardware address on the forwarded envelope. The office reads it only from that helper, and ignores it anywhere else.

sections.title: Client Behavior
sections.content: The option is only exchanged between relay agents and servers, so DHCPv6 clients are not aware of it. A client MUST NOT send the option, and MUST ignore it if it receives one.
sections.eli5: Only the helpers and the office use this note. You are never supposed to write one or read one.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
A rogue relay agent could insert a wrong link-layer address, and a DHCPv6 client could pose as a relay by sending a Relay-Forward message with a wrong option. A DHCPv6 client could then pass itself off as the same device as a DHCPv4 client.

The RFC's example is Dynamic DNS: a DHCPv4 client installs an A record (RFC 4702), and a masquerading DHCPv6 client installs an AAAA record with the same name (RFC 4704), so dual-stack nodes might connect to the wrong machine. Administrators of servers that use this option are strongly advised to secure server-to-relay traffic with IPsec, as in Section 21.1 of RFC 3315.

There is also a privacy angle. Where the network operator and the connectivity provider are separate, or the relay talks to the server over an open network, the option could reveal information. Operators are strongly recommended to use IPsec for confidentiality in those cases.
sections.eli5: If someone fakes the hardware address on the envelope, they could trick the office into thinking they are somebody else. Sealing the messages between helper and office protects against this.

fields.name: option-length
fields.desc: 2 plus the length of the link-layer address.

fields.name: link-layer address
fields.desc: The client's link-layer address; variable length.
